title: Centralized Generation of Electricity and its Impacts on the Environment | US EPA
content:
Centralized Generation of Electricity and its Impacts on the Environment
- About centralized generation
- Centralized generation in the United States
- Environmental impacts of centralized generation
About Centralized Generation
“Centralized generation” refers to the large-scale generation of electricity at centralized facilities. These facilities are usually located away from end-users and connected to a network of high-voltage transmission lines. The electricity generated by centralized generation is distributed through the electric power grid to multiple end-users. Centralized generation facilities include fossil-fuel-fired power plants, nuclear power plants, hydroelectric dams, wind farms, and more.
Centralized Generation in the United States
The vast majority of the electricity that Americans use is from centralized generation. Centralized generation facilities in the United States currently have the capacity to generate more than 1,100 gigawatts of electric power.
The earliest electric utilities operated independently from each other. A consumer would purchase electricity from a utility in their area, which would then provide the electricity through its own electricity delivery system. During the second half of the 20th century, utilities found it more efficient and economical to connect their delivery systems, resulting in the need to coordinate power plant operations. The majority of electricity generation in the United States today is coordinated by regional system operators to ensure reliability. Therefore, the electricity delivered to consumers by their local electric utility may be generated at a centralized power plant located in another city or state and owned by a different company. These power plants are subject to economic, reliability, and environmental regulations by federal, tribal, state, and/or local governments.
Environmental Impacts of Centralized Generation
The environmental impacts of electricity generation can contribute to large-scale regional environmental concerns as well as localized concerns that affect the area directly surrounding a power plant. Some impacts vary based on the energy resource—for example, whether the power plant uses fossil fuel or a renewable resource. In addition to the impacts from power generation, there are also impacts associated with extracting, producing, and transporting certain fuels such as coal and natural gas.
In general, centralized power plants can affect the environment in the following ways:
- Air pollutant emissions:
		
  - The amount and type of emissions will vary by fuel burned and other plant characteristics.
  - Air pollution from burning fuel often includes carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and particulate matter.
- Water use and discharge:
		
  - Water used for steam production or cooling may be returned at warmer temperatures to water bodies and may contain contaminants.
  - Some water may also be lost to evaporation.
- Waste generation:
		
  - Burning certain fuels results in solid waste such as ash, which must be stored and eventually disposed of properly.
  - Some wastes contain hazardous substances. For example, nuclear power generation produces radioactive waste, while coal ash can contain heavy metals like mercury.
- Land use:
		
  - Large power plants require space for their operations.
  - Centralized generation requires transmission lines, which also use land.
In addition to these environmental impacts, much of the primary energy (total energy content) of fossil fuels burned at power plants is wasted during generation and delivery to end-users. Opportunities exist to improve the energy efficiency of power plants, as well as to locate electricity generation closer to end-users to reduce losses during electricity delivery.

title: Research on the design and simulation of grid-connected system of vertical gravity energy storage - Scientific Reports
content:
Abstract
Due to the characteristics of the body’s movement, the output power of the gravity energy storage system is unstable. When the system is connected to the grid, smooth control of the output power is required. To this end, this paper proposes a control scheme that uses multiple units for joint power generation and complements the output power. The system operation parameters are optimized through an optimization algorithm to achieve power smoothing. The optimized gravity energy storage system can output stable power generation and can be equivalent to a controlled current source in grid-connected systems. Based on this, a corresponding gravity energy storage grid-connected system was designed, and the converter adopted a voltage-oriented vector control strategy for grid connection control. Subsequently, grid-connected system simulation and short-circuit fault simulation experiments were carried out. The simulation results show that the output power of the optimized gravity energy storage system is stable, and the minimum power fluctuation rate can reach 6.7%. The designed grid-connected system has a fast response speed and good steady-state characteristics. It can return to the original value after a sudden change of 0.4 s in the system input, so as to achieve the stable grid connection of the gravity energy storage system.
Similar content being viewed by others
Introduction
Against the backdrop of increasingly severe global energy shortages and environmental deterioration, renewable energy generation technologies such as solar and wind power have developed rapidly in recent years. However, due to the intermittency and volatility of renewable energy generation, its large-scale grid connection brings many challenges to the operation of the power system, including issues such as power quality and the consumption of new energy1. Energy storage systems can significantly improve energy utilization and facilitate new energy consumption. Because of this, they have become a key research focus in the development of new energy and power systems2,3,4.
Among various energy storage technologies, pumped storage is the most widely used, but it relies on the water environment and has high requirements for geographical location. Electrochemical energy storage has a high energy conversion efficiency and rapid response capability, but it has safety and thermal management issues and causes certain pollution to the environment. Flywheel energy storage has a long cycle life and low decay rate, but it has certain limitations on materials and is relatively expensive5,6. Gravity energy storage technology has developed on the basis of pumped storage. By changing the energy storage medium from water to solid, it reduces the dependence on site selection. Thanks to its advantages such as large-scale energy storage capacity, environmental friendliness, and flexible site selection, gravity energy storage technology has become a research hotspot in the current energy storage field, demonstrating significant development potential7,8. According to the differences in technical routes, gravity energy storage is mainly divided into piston type, shaft type, frame type and slope type, etc. Among them, the shaft type gravity energy storage technology can be built in abandoned mines and has the characteristics of small land occupation and stable structure. Compared with other forms, it is more feasible in engineering9,10,11.
Tens of thousands of abandoned mines were left in the UK’s midlands region. To address this, the British company Gravitricity first proposed the vertical shaft gravity energy storage technology. This scheme adopts the construction of gravity energy storage vertical shaft channels in abandoned mines, and uses electric winches to transport heavy objects to achieve energy storage and release. While reducing construction costs, it also solves the problem of mine resource waste12. Based on this, the company conducted a 250 kW vertical shaft gravity energy storage demonstration platform experiment in Edinburgh Lees Port in 2021. A 50-ton load was lifted to a 15-m mine platform and then dropped. The discharge process was completed within 1–2 s. This experiment verified the feasibility of vertical shaft gravity energy storage13. Meanwhile, the University of Oxford theoretically analyzed the vertical shaft gravity energy storage system, established a mathematical model of the system, analyzed and calculated the power generation characteristics and economy of the system, and verified the feasibility of vertical shaft gravity energy storage technology14. The Institute of Electrical Engineering of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has proposed a plan to use a hoist to lift multiple heavy objects. Through PLC, the hoist, track and lifting gear are intelligently controlled to achieve the automated operation of the system. In 2022, the charging and discharging performance tests of a 10KW-level vertical shaft gravity energy storage system were conducted. The system can operate automatically in island mode or grid-connected mode. In the design of grid-connected systems for gravity energy storage, the Chinese Academy of Sciences has proposed a technical solution for the grid-connected hybrid system of gravity energy storage and flywheel energy storage, taking advantage of the high instantaneous power and fast charging and discharging speed of flywheel energy storage to smooth the output power curve of gravity energy storage15. Guizhou University has proposed a voltage-oriented control strategy that conducts control on both the motor side and the grid side respectively, which can simulate and achieve the stable operation of the sloping gravity energy storage system after grid connection16,17.
At present, few studies have focused on the output power characteristics of gravity energy storage itself, and conducted grid connection control based on these characteristics in the field of grid-connected control and system optimization of siloed gravity energy storage. The gravity energy storage grid-connected system designed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Guizhou University achieves power smoothing by controlling the speed of the motor15,16,17. Wang et al. considered the inrush current during grid connection on this basis and achieved better control effects18. However, none of these studies took into account the stepped-changing output power characteristics of gravity energy storage, which increased the difficulty of control, and did not optimize the system operation parameters of gravity energy storage. Elasyed, Botha et al. optimized the system design parameters of gravity energy storage to achieve better energy storage efficiency19,20. Can Lv optimizes the capacity of gravity energy storage to achieve better economic efficiency21. These design optimizations focus more on the energy storage efficiency and economy of the gravity energy storage system itself, while neglecting the important indicator of the power generation capacity of the gravity energy storage system. Based on the above research, this paper innovatively focuses on the output power characteristics of gravity energy storage. By using optimization algorithms to optimize the operating parameters of the gravity energy storage system, the output power of the gravity energy storage system is controlled, and a multi-machine joint approach is adopted to achieve power smoothing, thereby enabling the grid connection of the gravity energy storage system. Achieving power smoothing before grid connection not only reduces the difficulty of motor control but also lessens the impact on the power grid caused by the frequent changes in the output power of gravity energy storage. Subsequently, this paper designs the corresponding gravity energy storage grid-connected system, and then conducts simulation experiments to verify the proposed gravity energy storage grid-connected system, and performs fault simulation.
Vertical shaft gravity energy storage system model
Gravity energy storage working principle
The components of the vertical shaft type gravity energy storage device are shown in Fig. 1, mainly including the vertical shaft channel for lifting heavy objects, the cage and the loaded heavy object blocks, the power electronic converter device, the motor and steel wire rope, and the transmission lifting system composed of the winch and pulley. The heavy block serves as the energy storage medium in the energy storage system. The change in its high and low positions enables the storage and release of energy. The converter plays a crucial role in the entire system. It serves as the channel for power flow between the gravity energy storage device and the power grid. This system transmits electrical energy between the motor and the power grid. During discharge, it sends electricity generated by the descending weight to the grid. During charging, it conveys excess grid electricity to the motor to lift the weight, thereby storing energy. The basic working principle of the vertical shaft gravity energy storage system is as follows: During energy storage, the excess electrical energy from the power grid is transmitted to the gravity energy storage system through a converter. The motor operates in the motor state, pulling the heavy block to rise, converting electrical energy into gravitational potential energy, and achieving energy storage. When releasing energy, the motor operates in the generator state. The descent of a heavy block pulls the motor to rotate, converting gravitational potential energy into electrical energy. This energy is then transmitted to the power grid through a converter, achieving the release of energy.
To accurately depict the power output characteristics of a gravity energy storage system, it is necessary to conduct a dynamic analysis of its core driving process—the falling of heavy objects. The output power needs to be smoothed. When power is superimposed, an optimization algorithm is adopted to optimize the falling velocity curve of the weight block during the operation of the gravity energy storage system, thereby achieving the purpose of reducing the power volatility after superimposition. As a long-duration energy storage, gravity energy storage has a relatively long single operation cycle and a long overall grid-connected operation time. The internal electromechanical dynamic process of the system has a relatively small impact on the overall steady-state power output of the system. Converter control strategy
In the grid-connected gravity energy storage system, the grid-side converter serves as the core unit and primarily performs two key functions: first, stabilizing the DC bus voltage, and second, regulating the active and reactive power delivered to the grid25,26,27. The converter typically adopts a dual-loop control strategy based on coordinate transformation, combined with Space Vector Pulse Width Modulation (SVPWM) technology to achieve efficient energy conversion. SVPWM controls the six sets of switching devices in the three-phase inverter to generate modulation waveforms with specific timing sequences, approximating an ideal sinusoidal current output. Its theoretical foundation lies in the principle of average value equivalence, where combinations of basic voltage vectors are used to achieve the same average value as the target voltage vector within a switching period.
The control strategies for the grid-side converter can be broadly categorized into two types based on the method of coordinate orientation: grid voltage-based control strategies and virtual flux-based control strategies. Among these, the grid voltage-based control strategies include voltage-oriented control and direct power control. This paper adopts the voltage-oriented control strategy based on grid voltage. This strategy relies on monitoring or estimating the grid voltage to regulate the d-axis and q-axis currents on the grid side, thereby maintaining the stability of the DC-side voltage. This enables decoupled control of active and reactive power, allowing independent regulation of active and reactive power. The principle of this control strategy is illustrated in Fig. 528.

Therefore, by independently controlling the d-axis and q-axis components of the grid current, decoupled control of active and reactive power can be achieved. Assuming negligible converter losses, maintaining the stability of the DC-side voltage ensures that all active power from the DC side is transferred to the grid, enabling precise regulation of both active and reactive power injected into the grid. In a two-phase synchronous rotating coordinate system, the voltage equation of the grid-side converter is:

The grid position Angle is obtained by detecting the grid voltage through the phase-locked loop (PLL).
The control of the d-axis and q-axis voltage and current employs a dual-loop proportional-integral (PI) control structure with an outer voltage loop and an inner current loop. The control circuit samples the DC-side voltage and the grid-side three-phase voltages/currents. The sampled values are compared with their reference values, and the resulting errors are processed through PI regulators to generate the SVPWM pulse signals, thereby achieving precise control of the converter. In this design, the reactive power is controlled to zero by setting the q-axis current reference value to 0. The decoupling algorithm is:

In terms of converters, the commonly used converters at present are IGBT and IGCT. IGBTs offer low conduction voltage drop and high blocking voltage capability, making them suitable for medium-power applications such as power conversion and variable-frequency drives. IGCTs, on the other hand, feature low switching losses and superior short-circuit withstand capability, making them ideal for high-power applications like high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission and motor drives. Compared to IGCTs, IGBTs have faster switching speeds, capable of reaching nanosecond-level transitions, thus being more suitable for high-frequency applications. However, IGCTs exhibit higher voltage withstand capability, reaching up to several kilovolts, while the withstand voltage of IGBTs typically ranges from a few hundred volts to several kilovolts, relatively lower. Additionally, IGCTs demonstrate excellent short-circuit tolerance, able to withstand high peak currents and large short-circuit energy. In contrast, IGBTs have weaker short-circuit capability and require external protection circuits to prevent overcurrent and overheating. Due to differences in structure and materials, IGCTs offer better thermal stability in high-temperature environments. They can operate at higher temperatures and have relatively lower cooling requirements. IGBTs, however, are prone to thermal runaway under high temperatures and require additional cooling mechanisms to maintain stable operation.
In addition, in terms of losses, due to the large power level and current, conduction loss plays a dominant role. The conduction losses of IGBT and IGCT can be expressed as:

Given the high power level of the gravity energy storage system in this design, which involves large currents. The on-state voltage drop of IGCT is about 0.5 to 1 V less than that of IGBT. When the current size is 5000A, the loss of IGBT increases by 2500W. So, IGCTs are selected for the inverter.
Analysis of simulation results
Grid-connected system simulation
Based on the mathematical models and control principles outlined in Chapters 1 and 2, a simulation model of the grid-connected gravity energy storage system was built in MATLAB/Simulink, and experimental validation was conducted. The topology of the constructed simulation model is shown in Fig. 6.
The gravity energy storage system is equivalently represented as a controlled current source, which is connected to an inverter that converts DC power into three-phase AC power. After passing through reactors and transformers, it is connected to the three-phase power supply for grid connection. The bus voltage signal on the DC side and the phase current and phase voltage signals on the grid-connected side are sampled. The sampled signals are input into the control circuit for double closed-loop SVPWM control, and the output PWM signal is used to control the three-phase inverter. The system parameter Settings of the gravity energy storage system are shown in Table 2.
According to the set parameters, a grid-connected system simulation model is built, and the initial output power of the gravity energy storage module is set at 40 MW, then it suddenly changed to 20 MW after 5 s. After the system runs for 10 s, the voltage on the DC side is shown in Fig. 7a, and the active power on the converter side is shown in Fig. 7b.
As can be seen from Fig. 7a, after the simulation starts, due to the excessive power level, the DC bus voltage increases rapidly and overshoot occurs. After dropping and rising, it remains stable. After a total response time of 1 s, the DC voltage stabilizes at around the given value of 8000 V, with a steady-state error of ± 50 V, which is 0.63% of the given value. According to the theory of vector control, when the bus voltage on the DC side remains constant, all the active power on the DC side is transmitted to the grid-connected side through the converter. The active power on the converter side is shown in Fig. 7b. It can be seen from Fig. 7b that the active power on the converter side varies with the variation of the bus voltage on the DC side. When the bus voltage on the DC side remains stable, the active power on the converter side also remains stable at 40 MW. The output power of the gravity energy storage system has been fully transmitted to the grid-connected side. The effectiveness of the control strategy has been verified, which can stably transmit the 40 MW high-power output of the gravity energy storage module. All the active power on the DC side flows into the voltage, meeting the power requirements for grid connection. All the active power on the DC side flows into the voltage, meeting the power requirements for grid connection.
When the input power undergoes a sudden change within 5 s, the bus voltage and active power on the DC side drop rapidly. After a response time of 0.4 s, they rise rapidly to reach a new stability. The bus voltage on the DC side remains at around 8000 V after the input power change, with a steady-state error of ± 50 V. The active power on the converter side stabilizes at 20 MW. It can be seen that when there is a sudden change in the system input, the designed control link can well regulate and maintain the stability of the bus voltage on the DC side. All the active power on the DC side flows into the power grid, meeting the power requirements for grid connection.
After the active power is transmitted to the grid-connected side through the converter, it is boosted by the transformer and connected to the power grid. The rated voltage on the secondary side of the transformer is 690 V. After the system stabilizes, the voltage and current waveforms on the grid side are shown in Fig. 8.
As can be seen in Fig. 8, the three-phase voltage and three-phase current on the grid side remain stable after a response time of 0.15 s. The waveforms are stable sine waves with small harmonics, and the THD of the three-phase voltage is 4.72%, and the designed gravity energy storage system can achieve stable grid connection operation. When the input power undergoes a sudden change within 5 s, the three-phase voltage waveform on the grid side remains basically stable, and the THD of the three-phase voltage is 4.72% before and after the system input sudden change. The three-phase current waveforms on the grid side decrease after a sudden change in the system input, and then rise and remain stable after a very short period of time. By combining the stable DC side bus voltage and the active power waveform flowing into the grid side in Fig. 7, it can be seen that the designed system has good control performance, and the control strategy is effective, which can achieve stable grid connection of the gravity energy storage system.
Next, the output power will be continuously changed from 40 to 20 MW. After the system is in operation, the DC voltage waveform and the active power waveform of the converter are shown in Fig. 9.
As can be seen from Fig. 9, after adopting the continuously changing power command, the DC bus voltage can also remain stable, stabilizing at around the given value of 8000 V. The active power on the converter side also decreases as the power command drops, and all the active power on the DC side flows into the grid side to achieve the transmission of active power.
Figure 10 shows the grid-side voltage and current diagrams when the power command continuously varies from 40 to 20 MW. It can be seen that the grid-side voltage remains stable, with a sine wave waveform and a THD of 4.93%. The current on the grid side also remains stable. The system also has excellent control performance when the power command changes continuously, and can achieve stable grid connection of the gravity energy storage system.
In addition, after power optimization for gravity energy storage systems at different power levels, the power fluctuation rates also varies, as detailed in Table 3. The power waveform diagrams of the optimized power levels of 30, 34, 40, and 42 MW are shown in Fig. 11.
From the above table, it can be observed that when the power level exceeds a certain value, the fluctuation rate increases with the rise in power level. If the gravity energy storage system is required to deliver higher output power to achieve greater power utilization, the power fluctuation rate will consequently increase.
Fault simulation
In grid-connected systems, simulating and analyzing various types of short-circuit faults is critically important. Through such simulations and analyses, the dynamic response of the power system under fault conditions can be predicted, providing a theoretical basis for subsequent fault handling and system design. In the simulation model of the grid-connected gravity energy storage system, a fault module was introduced to simulate single-phase-to-ground short-circuit faults, double-phase-to-ground short-circuit faults, and phase-to-phase short-circuit faults. The faults were applied at the transformer side, connected to the converter and reactor. During the fault simulation experiments, the phase voltages, phase currents, and short-circuit currents at the fault location were measured, and the simulation results were analyzed.
In the simulation model, a single-phase-to-ground fault was set to occur at 2 s, with phase A selected as the faulted phase. The voltage and current waveforms at the fault location obtained from the simulation are shown in Fig. 12.
From Fig. 12, it can be observed that after the fault occurs in 2 s, the voltage of the faulted phase A decreases rapidly, while its current surges to a very high peak. The voltages and currents of the non-faulted phases remain unchanged. Next, a double-phase-to-ground short-circuit fault experiment is conducted. The fault type is set as a double-phase-to-ground short-circuit fault, with Phase A and Phase B selected as the faulted phases. The fault is set to occur at 2 s. The voltage and current waveforms at the fault location obtained from the simulation are shown in Fig. 13.
From Fig. 13, it can be observed that after the fault occurs at t = 2 s, the voltages of the faulted phases A and B decrease rapidly, while their currents surge to very high peaks. The voltages and currents of the non-faulted phase remain unchanged. A phase-to-phase short-circuit fault experiment is then conducted. The fault type is set as a phase-to-phase short-circuit fault between Phase A and Phase B. The fault is initiated at t = 2 s, and the resulting voltage and current waveforms at the fault location are shown in Fig. 14.
From Fig. 14, it can be observed that after the phase-to-phase short-circuit fault occurs in 2 s, the voltages of the faulted phases A and B decrease significantly, while their currents surge rapidly to very high and equal peaks. The voltage and current of the non-faulted phase remain unchanged. The DC-side voltage and active power waveforms after the fault occurrence are shown in Fig. 15.
From Fig. 15, it can be observed that after the fault occurs, both the DC-side bus voltage and the converter’s active power undergo sudden changes. After a period of adjustment, they eventually recover to stable states. The DC-side bus voltage drops to approximately 6500 V, while the active power on the converter side decreases to around 33 MW.
Conclusion and discussion
Based on the working principle of gravity energy storage, this paper establishes a mathematical model of the power generation output for the gravity energy storage system. To address the instability of single-unit power generation, a grid-connected scheme utilizing multiple units in combination is proposed to achieve complementary power output and ensure stable power delivery. Simulation experiments of the grid-connected system and fault scenarios were conducted. The results indicate:
- 
                  (1)
                  
                    The optimized gravity energy storage system achieves stable power output. Within the power range of 30–44 MW, the fluctuation rate remains below 9% after optimization, reaching a minimum of 6.7% at 30 MW.
- 
                  (2)
                  
                    The optimized gravity energy storage system can be equivalently represented as a controlled current source in the grid-connected model. However, within a certain range, the greater the output power of the gravity energy storage system, the higher the power fluctuation rate may be, such as 30-36 MW and 38-42 MW, which will affect the stability of grid connection.
- 
                  (3)
                  
                    The simulation results of the gravity energy storage grid-connected system show that under the designed control links, the grid-connected system has a fast response speed and good steady-state characteristics. After a response time of 1 s, the DC side voltage can reach approximately 8000 V of the control set value, with a steady-state error of about ± 50 V, which is 0.65% of the set value. And it can return to the original value 0.4 s after a sudden change occurs in the system input. The voltage and current waveforms on the grid side are stable. The THD of the grid-side voltage is 4.72%. When there is a sudden change in the system input, the grid-side current stabilizes after 0.4 s, which enables the stable grid connection of the gravity energy storage system. The simulation results of short-circuit faults show that when a fault occurs in the line, the current of the faulty phase increases rapidly, and the voltage of the faulty phase decreases accordingly and then reaches a new steady state.
As a new type of energy storage system, gravity energy storage systems not only can solve the contradiction between power supply and demand, but also are conducive to the economic and safe operation of the power grid. Vertical shafts can be excavated vertically downward, making full use of underground space and reducing the occupation of surface land. They can also be combined with other facilities such as underground parking lots and civil air defense projects for construction, further enhancing the comprehensive utilization efficiency of land. Under the condition of saving construction costs by adopting abandoned mines, the levelized cost per kilowatt-hour can reach 171$/kWh, and the service life is about 50 to 60 years. In addition, the system efficiency can reach 80%, which is higher than that of pumped storage. The fact that it does not pollute the environment is also an advantage that electrochemical energy storage does not have. However, due to the inherent movement characteristics of the vertical shaft type gravity energy storage system, there are problems such as frequent start and stop of multiple motors, stepwise power changes, and poor power quality when responding to continuous power regulation instructions. Therefore, it is necessary to achieve continuous and smooth power control of multiple motors within the gravity energy storage system through the optimization of control strategies. However, when multi-unit coordinated control is adopted, the multi-unit parallel circulation problem during the charging and discharging operation of the gravity energy storage system will be an engineering challenge that needs to be solved in the future.

title: 83,000-pound Tesla battery coming to Huntsville Utilities power grid
content:
HUNTSVILLE — Huntsville Utilities has taken delivery of an 83,000-pound battery that will serve as the first grid-scale battery project of its kind in North Alabama, part of a pilot effort aimed at managing peak electric demand during extreme weather.
“It’s about the size of the back end of a semi,” said Todd Long of Huntsville Utilities. “It actually wasn’t supposed to be delivered until the summer, but they called and said they had time to send it early, so we went ahead and took it.
“Right now it’s being stored at our Triana facility while we prepare the site, which was already planned for later this year.”
The battery is part of a grid load management project funded in part by a grant from the American Public Power Association and will be installed at the Stringfield Substation near Pulaski Pike.
“This is a pilot project to learn more about how we would control the charging and discharging of the battery,” said Stacy Cantrell, Huntsville Utilities’ vice president of engineering. “We do expect to eventually install batteries at other substations.”
The battery, manufactured by Tesla, will store electricity during off-peak hours and discharge power during periods of high demand, such as extreme heat or extreme cold. The goal is to reduce stress on transformers and other grid equipment by easing overloads during peak usage.
According to Huntsville Utilities engineer Anyama Tettey, who spearheaded the grant application, the battery is rated at 2 megawatts and 4 megawatt-hours, or 2MW/4MWh, with a maximum capacity of 2,400 kVA.
“For this particular project, we do not expect to output more than 1,900 kVA during a discharge cycle,” Tettey said. “This will avoid excessive battery degradation.”
The battery will serve the portion of the electric grid connected to the Stringfield Substation, an area selected in part because it already has sufficient space and infrastructure to support the installation. It can also provide limited assistance during outages affecting that section of the system.
The $125,000 grant from the American Public Power Association covers a large portion of the cost of the system. Tettey said Huntsville Utilities will also receive tax credits tied to the installation.
“This is the first project of its kind in north Alabama,” Tettey said. “EPB in Chattanooga has a similar battery, but their use is different from what we will be using ours for.”
Installation is planned for next year, with the system expected to be operational by summer. Looking ahead, Huntsville Utilities sees battery storage as a potential long-term tool for managing growth and rising demand.
“Our goal is to shave off the peak during the on-peak period,” Tettey said. “The more batteries we have that would allow us to do that, the better. Each battery size would have to be site specific.”
The system will be charged during off-peak hours and discharged on days when peak demand is anticipated, based on weather forecasts and historical usage data, particularly during temperature extremes.
